findings.section: How it works > ACM certificates are Regional and CloudFront reads them only from us-east-1
findings.quote: 2. **CloudFront to the load balancer.** You can [import the certificate in any AWS Region](../facts/acm.md#acm-cloudfront-origin-certificate-any-region) for the origin.
findings.evidence: acm-faq-certificate-same-region-as-resource: 'must be in the same Region' / 'The only exception is Amazon CloudFront'. Read literally, 'any AWS Region' tells the reader the load balancer's certificate can live in a Region other than the load balancer's, which contradicts the table four lines below ('Its own: it must be in the same Region'). The fact acm-cloudfront-origin-certificate-any-region means only 'not tied to us-east-1'. Say: the origin certificate sits in the load balancer's own Region, which need not be US East (N. Virginia).
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): Step 2 now reads 'The origin certificate [must be in the same Region](acm-faq-certificate-same-region-as-resource) as the load balancer.' It agrees with the table.

findings.section: secrets-certificates-q002 (5-quiz.md Question 3) > Why
findings.quote: The load balancer keeps its eu-west-1 certificate, because you can [import the certificate in any AWS Region](../facts/acm.md#acm-cloudfront-origin-certificate-any-region) for the origin.
findings.evidence: Same defect as reader-01. The real reason the eu-west-1 certificate stays is acm-faq-certificate-same-region-as-resource ('must be in the same Region'); 'any AWS Region' teaches the opposite rule for the load balancer and invites a wrong answer on a twin where the load balancer moves Region.
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): q002 explanation now ends 'because a load balancer's certificate [must be in the same Region](acm-faq-certificate-same-region-as-resource) as the load balancer.' Explanation only; stem, options and key unchanged, so no new verification.

findings.section: secrets-certificates-s01 > ten_second

findings.evidence: secrets-manager-ecs-compare-parameter-store: both 'use AWS KMS to encrypt sensitive data'; parameter-store-three-parameter-types and 2-deep.md ('A sensitive value goes into a SecureString') show String and StringList are not encrypted. The 10-second answer is the line she memorizes and says to a CTO; 'encrypt them' claims every Parameter Store value is KMS-encrypted. Use the 60-second wording: 'both encrypt the sensitive ones with AWS KMS'.
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): s01 ten_second now reads 'Both store values and encrypt the sensitive ones with AWS KMS. Secrets Manager also rotates passwords. Put credentials there, and plain configuration in Parameter Store.' (25 words).

findings.section: secrets-certificates-s01 > sixty_second line 5
findings.quote: Secrets Manager rotates the password with a Lambda function.
findings.evidence: secrets-manager-managed-rotation-no-lambda and secrets-manager-managed-rotation-rds-master-user; 2-deep.md teaches that for an RDS master password managed rotation needs no Lambda function (the LEAST-overhead exam signal). Callvale runs Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL (STARTUP.md stage 1), so the model answer gives Ben the higher-overhead path. Say: 'Secrets Manager rotates the password; for RDS, RDS can manage it for you.'
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): s01 line 5 now reads 'Secrets Manager rotates the password. For Amazon RDS, RDS can manage that for you.'

findings.section: secrets-certificates-s01 > key_points kp3 (must) and sixty_second line 7
findings.quote: And you still get one place. The application can read the secret through a Parameter Store reference.
findings.evidence: parameter-store-reference-secrets-manager-prefix ('/aws/reference/secretsmanager/'). A 'must' key point that neither 1-fast.md nor 2-deep.md mentions: the reader meets the reference for the first time in the model answer and cannot explain it if Ben asks how. Add one sentence (or a Go deeper line) in the Parameter Store subsection, or make kp3 'nice'.
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): kp3 is now 'nice' (must points kp1, kp2, kp4). The line is shorter: 'You still get one place: a Parameter Store reference can point to the secret.' No prose sentence was added: 2-deep.md is at its word cap.

findings.section: secrets-certificates-s02 > sixty_second line 9
findings.quote: And if someone deletes the record, renewal is no longer automatic.
findings.evidence: acm-faq-remove-cname-stops-renewal: ACM 'cannot issue or renew certificates' with DNS validation 'if you remove the CNAME record'. 'No longer automatic' implies a manual renewal still happens; the true consequence is that the certificate expires unless the record is added back (2-deep.md Stop and answer says so). Say: 'If someone deletes the record, ACM cannot renew it, and the certificate expires.'
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): s02 line 9 now reads 'If someone deletes the record, ACM can't renew it, and the certificate expires.'

findings.section: How it works > Cross-account access to a secret needs a customer managed KMS key (heading)
findings.quote: ### Cross-account access to a secret needs a customer managed KMS key (4 min)
findings.evidence: secrets-manager-cross-account-needs-both-policies ('a resource policy and in an identity policy'); exemplar README item 3 (a heading must carry the rule). A skimmer learns 'a customer managed key is enough' from the heading, which is the mirror image of the trap the section warns about, and Q8 (q007) needs both the key and the resource-based policy. Heading should name both, for example 'Cross-account access to a secret needs a resource-based policy and a customer managed KMS key'.
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): The H3 heading texts are fixed by brief.json (TOOLS-rules R4; L905 and the section ids of items depend on them), so a writer cannot rename it; the orchestrator owns the brief. The first line under the heading now says 'A reader in another account needs three allows.', and the truth table has the row with aws/secretsmanager that fails (reader-08).

findings.section: How it works > Cross-account access ... > truth table
findings.quote: | Other account | Allows | Silent | Allows the reader | Fails |
findings.evidence: secrets-manager-cross-account-no-aws-managed-key and secrets-manager-aws-managed-key-policy-fixed; exemplar README item 2 (the truth table carries the rule for a skimmer). The table has no row for the most-tested failure: other account, both policies allow, key aws/secretsmanager -> Fails. Add that row so the skim gives the key half of the rule.
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): The table has the row 'Other account | Allows | Allows the reader | aws/secretsmanager | Fails'.

findings.section: How it works > Cross-account access ... > step 1
findings.quote: 1. **Encrypt.** Secrets Manager [requests a new data key from AWS KMS](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-envelope-encryption-data-key) (AWS Key Management Service) for each new value.
findings.evidence: Rule: STYLE/CONVENTIONS term before use and cause-and-effect. 'Data key' is never explained, and the step does not say why it matters for a cross-account reader (the reader must be allowed to use the KMS key to decrypt). The link to step 3 is left for the reader to infer. Replace with one plain cause: 'The secret is encrypted with a KMS key, so a reader must also be allowed to decrypt with that key.'
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): Step 1 now starts 'Secrets Manager encrypts each value', and step 3 states the cause: 'The reader also uses the KMS key, so [the key policy must give the external account permission].' 'data key' stays as the AWS term inside the link text (display).

findings.section: How it works > Cross-account access ... > Exam trap
findings.quote: If the secret uses aws/secretsmanager, keep the secret: you can [change the encryption key for your secret](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-change-kms-key-reencrypts-labeled).
findings.evidence: STYLE plain-English rule (no compressed phrasing). 'keep the secret' is ambiguous for a second-language reader (keep it private? keep it unchanged?). It means 'you do not need to create a new secret'. Write that.
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): Now reads 'If the secret uses aws/secretsmanager, you need no new secret: you can [change the encryption key for your secret].'

findings.section: How it works > Secrets Manager replaces a stored password ... > step 1
findings.quote: 1. **Move.** Move the password into a **secret**, and [then rotate them immediately](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-move-hardcoded-then-rotate).
findings.evidence: secrets-manager-move-hardcoded-then-rotate: the claim includes 'revokes the current hardcoded password'. The sentence has a pronoun error ('password ... them') and drops the reason: the old password still sits in every copy of the file until a rotation replaces it. The reason is what lets her explain the step to a customer.
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): Step 1 now reads 'Move the credentials into a **secret**, and [then rotate them immediately].' (pronoun fixed). The reason stands in the subsection's first line: 'A password in a configuration file does not change, and it leaks with every copy.' A further clause did not fit the word cap (2,399 of 2,400).

findings.section: In one breath > hero steps; also 2-deep.md step 3
findings.quote: 3. Secrets Manager returns the AWSCURRENT version over TLS.
findings.evidence: Rule: CONVENTIONS term introduced before use. AWSCURRENT and 'staging label' appear in the fast file and in deep step 3 with no plain meaning; the reader first learns what a version label does in the rotation table two subsections later (AWSPENDING / finishSecret). Add a half-sentence: 'AWSCURRENT is the label on the version that applications should use now.'
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): In 2-deep step 3 the term is now explained ('[returns that version by default], the version with the staging label AWSCURRENT'). The 1-fast hero steps must equal the diagram spec `say` text (L702, L703), which brief.json fixes (R4); changing them needs a brief and diagram change by the orchestrator.

findings.section: How it works > Automatic rotation ... > step 2
findings.quote: Otherwise Secrets Manager [calls the same function several times](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-rotation-function-called-per-step), one time for each step.
findings.evidence: Rule: term before use. 'The same function' refers to a rotation Lambda function that the text never introduced; 'window' in step 1 ('in a window of at least one hour') is also undefined. Name it: 'Otherwise a Lambda rotation function does the work, and Secrets Manager calls it once for each step.'
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): Now reads 'Otherwise a Lambda rotation function runs: Secrets Manager [calls the same function several times], one call per step.'

findings.section: How it works > Automatic rotation ... > Why
findings.quote: Why steps? If a step fails, Secrets Manager [retries the entire rotation process multiple times](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-rotation-retries-in-window) during the window.
findings.evidence: Exemplar README item 4 (one real 'Why does AWS work this way?' reason). The answer describes retry, not why rotation is split into steps. The cause the table already supports: the new password is tested (testSecret on AWSPENDING) before AWSCURRENT moves (finishSecret), so readers never get an untested password. Say that, with the existing facts.
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): Now reads 'Why steps? The new password is tested before AWSCURRENT moves to it.' (the table rows testSecret and finishSecret carry the links).

findings.section: How it works > Automatic rotation ... > Exam trap
findings.quote: A rotation is not a redeploy, and [the open database connection is not re-authenticated](../facts/secrets-manager.md#secrets-manager-faq-rotation-open-connections).
findings.evidence: secrets-manager-faq-rotation-open-connections: 'Authentication happens when a connection is established'. The cause is dropped, and the consequence for the application is never stated, although the Say it ('how the application reconnects') and the decision record ('reconnects after a rotation') rely on it. Add the cause and one sentence on what the application does: on a new connection or an authentication failure, read the secret again.
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): The trap now reads 'A rotation is not a redeploy. [Authentication happens when a connection is established], so new connections read the secret again.' q003 explanation adds 'After a failed login, the application reads the secret again.'

findings.section: How it works > ACM certificates are Regional ... > Why
findings.quote: Why is CloudFront different? ACM has its one certificate [distributed to all the geographic locations](../facts/acm.md#acm-cloudfront-us-east-1) of the distribution.
findings.evidence: acm-cloudfront-us-east-1 states only that the certificate is requested in US East (N. Virginia) and then distributed; it does not give a reason, so the 'Why' answer is a restatement. The English is also awkward ('ACM has its one certificate distributed'). Rewrite as a plain statement: 'CloudFront is not in one Region. ACM takes the one certificate from US East (N. Virginia) and distributes it to all CloudFront locations.'
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): Now reads 'Why is CloudFront different? It is not in one Region: its certificate is [distributed to all the geographic locations] of the distribution.'

findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): Check 1 now changes the variable: 'A load balancer in Ireland is a CloudFront origin. Which Region holds its certificate?' findings.section: secrets-certificates-q006 (5-quiz.md Question 5) > Why not, option 3

findings.section: Words that go together
findings.quote: | encryption in transit | **attach** a TLS certificate to a listener | TLS encrypts the connection; the certificate proves who owns the domain name | encryption of stored data |
findings.evidence: READER.md: she forgets terminology under stress and needs collocations. Four rows only (SPEC allows 5), none for ACM verbs she must say out loud ('request a certificate', 'validate a domain', 'import / reimport a certificate') or for 'SecureString parameter'; the term column 'encryption in transit' does not match its collocation about a certificate, and 'listener' is unexplained in the fast file. No English vocabulary (term/word) cards exist in cards.json either.
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): A new words row needs a term of data/terms.json (L503), which the orchestrator owns, and 1-fast.md is near its 1,000-word cap after the fixes. Term and partner cards are generated by `cards build` from terms.json (R5), not written into cards.json. Note for the orchestrator: ACM collocations ('request a certificate', 'validate a domain', 'reimport a certificate').

findings.section: How it works > ACM certificates are Regional ... > Stop and answer
findings.quote: Two: one in [US East (N. Virginia)](../facts/acm.md#acm-cloudfront-us-east-1) for CloudFront, and one in US West (Oregon) for the load balancer.
findings.evidence: STARTUP.md line 20: Callvale builds in US East (N. Virginia). Every example puts the origin outside us-east-1, so the reader may over-learn 'CloudFront always needs a second certificate' and then advise Ben wrongly. One Go deeper line (or a Check variant) on an origin in us-east-1, where one certificate in that Region meets both rules (acm-cloudfront-us-east-1 plus acm-faq-certificate-same-region-as-resource), would test real reasoning. The file also switches between 'us-east-1' (heading) and 'US East (N. Virginia)' (body) without saying once that they are the same Region.
findings.resolution: fix-07 (2026-10-13): The us-east-1 origin case would claim that one certificate serves both CloudFront and the load balancer; no verified fact holds that, and 2-deep.md is at its word cap. The table row 'API Gateway, edge-optimized | US East (N. Virginia) – us-east-1 Region' ties the two names together.
